 Jeffries Promises a Fast ACA Subsidy Vote. It Will Miss the Dec. 15 Deadline
 Jeffries says restoring the enhanced ACA subsidy is an early House vote. For a single 64-year-old in her last year before Medicare, it would cut her 2027 premium from $19,803 to $5,950, but it cannot pass before the Dec. 15…
 By Jeremy Phillips 
 Published November 7, 2026, 6:04pm ET · 5 min read 
 𝕏 
 f 
 ⧉ 
 Quick Read
 Jeffries says the new House will vote early to restore the enhanced ACA subsidy, which capped the benchmark plan at 8.5% of income with no income limit.
 For a single 64-year-old drawing $70,000 from her IRA in 2027, restored rules would cut her benchmark premium from $19,803 to $5,950, but the new Congress is sworn in Jan. 3, after the Dec. 15 deadline for Jan. 1 coverage.
 Taking $62,000 from the IRA and $8,000 from savings keeps her under the $63,840 line under today's rules, saving about $14,564 in premium and tax.

 Hakeem Jeffries, in line to become House speaker, says restoring the enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidy will be among the first votes of the new House majority. “We’re going to get out of the gate fast,” he said, according to the AP.
 Consider a single retiree who is 64 for all of 2027. She turns 65 in January 2028, so 2027 is her last year buying a marketplace plan before Medicare. She has $700,000 in a traditional IRA and $60,000 in savings, and she planned to pull $70,000 from the IRA next year to cover everything. The benchmark silver plan for a 64-year-old at the national average runs about $1,650 a month, or $19,803 a year.
 The direct answer: if the vote passes and applies to 2027, it is worth $13,853 to her, cutting her premium from $19,803 to $5,950. But it cannot pass before her Dec. 15 enrollment deadline. The move that pays under either outcome is to enroll by Dec. 15 with $62,000 from the IRA and $8,000 from savings, which keeps her under the $63,840 subsidy line and saves about $14,564 whether or not Congress acts.
 What Jeffries said and what the vote would bring back
 The AP reported Nov. 7 that House Democratic leaders expect the new Congress, sworn in Jan. 3, to take early votes on boosting Medicaid and restoring the enhanced ACA premium tax credit. The enhanced rules ran from 2021 to 2025. They capped the benchmark silver plan at 8.5% of income and removed the income limit entirely. They expired Dec. 31, 2025.
 For 2027 coverage, the original rules are back. A household between 300% and 400% of the poverty level pays at most 10.22% of income for the benchmark plan, according to the IRS. Above 400% of poverty, which is $63,840 for one person in the 48 states and D.C., there is no credit at all. One dollar over the line erases the whole subsidy.
 The final bill’s terms, start date and length have not been written. Nothing public says a restored credit would reach back to Jan. 1, 2027.
 What she pays at five incomes, today versus restored
 Here is her benchmark cost at five 2027 incomes, under today’s rules first and the restored 8.5% cap second:
 $62,000 of income: $6,336 today, $5,091 restored.
 $63,840 of income: $6,524 today, $5,426 restored.
 $70,000 of income: $19,803 today, $5,950 restored.
 $80,000 of income: $19,803 today, $6,800 restored.
 $100,000 of income: $19,803 today, $8,500 restored.
 The pattern is the whole story. Under today’s rules, crossing $63,840 costs her the entire $13,278 credit. Under the restored rules, the credit shrinks gradually and would run out only around $233,000 of income for her, because 8.5% of that figure equals the full premium. At her planned $70,000, she sits $6,160 over the line, pays the full $19,803, and spends 28.3% of her income on health insurance. The vote would drop that to $5,950, or $496 a month, a saving of $1,154 a month.
 The calendar the vote has to clear
 You have 38 days from Nov. 7 to Dec. 15, the last day on HealthCare.gov to enroll or change plans for coverage starting Jan. 1. Open enrollment runs to Jan. 15, but a plan picked after Dec. 15 does not start Jan. 1.
 The new Congress is sworn in Jan. 3, 19 days after that deadline. Then the bill needs 60 votes in the Senate, and on election night Trump posted a photo of a red hat reading “VETO.” The extension passed the House in the current Congress with some Republican support and stalled in the Senate. Schumer says he sees initial signs that some Republicans could back restoring the enhanced subsidies.
 So she must pick a plan and report a 2027 income before any vote happens, and she should plan as if 2027 stays under the current rules.
 The move that works under either outcome
 Option 1: keep the $70,000 IRA draw and enroll by Dec. 15. She pays the full $19,803 unless the enhanced rules pass and apply to 2027. This fits someone who cannot reach the line any other way, and it is a bet on the Senate and a signature.
 Option 2: take $62,000 from the IRA and $8,000 from savings. Money from a savings account is already taxed and adds nothing to her modified adjusted gross income. She lands at $62,000, which is $1,840 under the line and 388.5% of poverty. Under today’s rules she pays 10.22% of income, $6,336 a year or $528 a month, instead of $19,803. That is $13,466 of premium saved. Her federal income tax also falls, from $6,290 at $70,000 to $5,192 at $62,000 (after the $16,600 standard deduction for a single filer), another $1,098. Total: about $14,564, and she still has $70,000 to spend. Her savings drop to $52,000. If the enhanced rules come back for 2027, her share falls to 8.21% of income, or $5,091, and she pockets another $1,245. This is the right call for her.
 Option 3: wait past Dec. 15 to see the vote. She loses Jan. 1 coverage, and the vote still faces the Senate and a veto. There is no documented payoff for waiting.
 Jeffries’ promise matters to her only for its upside. It does not change what she should do in the next 38 days.
 Run the numbers on your own account
 Find your benchmark silver premium. At the national average, multiply $703 by your age factor and divide by 1.278; for 64 the factor is 3.000, giving $1,650 a month.
 Find your line: 400% of the poverty guideline for your household size, $63,840 for one person.
 Add up your planned 2027 income: IRA withdrawals, interest, dividends, pension and all of your Social Security.
 If you are over the line, find the excess (here $6,160) and ask whether cash or a Roth account can replace that many IRA dollars.
 Your premium under the line is at most 10.22% of income, so $62,000 of income times 0.1022 equals $6,336. Your saving is the full premium minus that figure.
 Where this is weak
 The repayment risk is the big one. Starting with tax year 2026, the IRS says there is no cap on repaying excess advance premium tax credits. If a late IRA withdrawal, a Roth conversion, or a surprise capital gain pushes her final 2027 income over $63,840, she repays the full $13,466 advance credit at tax time. A cushion of $1,840 is thin. Anyone who cannot control income to the dollar should aim lower.
 The $1,650 premium is a national average times the federal 3-to-1 age curve. Real premiums vary by county, and some states use their own age curves, so her local number could be higher or lower.
 The restored rules may never apply to 2027. If the bill passes but starts in 2028, she gets nothing from it, since she will be on Medicare by then.
 The shift does not fit everyone. A retiree who needs $100,000 of income from an IRA has no cash swap that reaches the line, and only the vote helps that person. A retiree with no savings outside the IRA cannot substitute at all. Anyone already on Medicare, or whose Social Security and wages alone top $63,840, is outside this plan.
 The bottom line
 The vote Jeffries promises would cap her benchmark plan at 8.5% of income and end the cliff, worth $13,853 at her planned income. It cannot happen before Dec. 15. She should enroll by then with $62,000 from the IRA and $8,000 from savings, saving about $14,564 under current law. The one number to guard all year is $63,840: cross it by a dollar and the whole credit comes back as a tax bill.
